note: Verdicts on strings the distinctness checker cannot score. A line with fewer than four expressive words is almost entirely proper nouns and compelled vocabulary, and on those no metric can tell independent convergence from copying -- so each one gets read and dispositioned here by hand. `check` fails a book if any of its merger items is missing from this file, which keeps the unscoreable bucket from becoming a silent pass.
test: Would a second translator, working only from the public-domain Sanskrit and never having seen the fixture, arrive at substantially the same words? Where the answer is yes, the overlap is subject matter -- merger, or scenes a faire -- and carries no protectable expression. Where the answer is no, the line was rewritten instead of dispositioned.

merger.dhyanabindu/1.107/body_hi: nidravastha-madhye svapnavastha bhavati -- 'within the state of sleep, the dream state occurs'. A four-word structural sutra naming the nesting of two compelled technical terms (निद्रा, स्वप्न) already fixed by every earlier verse in this passage; Hindi has one ordinary way to say 'X occurs within Y' and no second vocabulary for these two states.
merger.muktika/2.33/body_hi: मन का नाश दो प्रकार का है: सरूप और अरूप -- a two-term technical classification (sa-rupa / a-rupa dissolution of mind) mapped to jivanmukti / dehamukti, the compelled Sanskrit pairing this whole passage turns on. There is no second way to name this binary distinction in Hindi; any translator restates the same four technical nouns in the same order.
merger.dhyanabindu/1.53/body_hi: gandhari hastijihva cha pusha chaiva yashasvini alambusa kuhur atra shankhini dashami smrita -- the same seven-name channel roll-call as yogachudamani/1.17, in the source's own fixed order, closed by the compelled gloss दसवीं (tenth). A list of names is the same list in any translation, and Hindi has no second way to transliterate these proper nouns.
merger.yogachudamani/1.17/body_en: gandhari hastijihva cha pusha chaiva yashasvini alambusa kuhush chaiva shankhini dashami smrita -- seven consecutive proper nouns naming channels, in the Sanskrit's own order, closed by the compelled gloss 'tenth'. A list of names is the same list in any translation.
merger.yogachudamani/1.17/body_hi: Same seven-name roll-call in Devanagari, in the source's fixed order. Hindi has no second way to transliterate these proper nouns.
merger.gopalatapani/3.16/body_hi: gopalo'hamajo nityah pradyumno'ham sanatanah -- 'I am Gopala, unborn, eternal; I am Pradyumna, everlasting'. Four compelled name/epithet pairs (Gopala, unborn, eternal, Pradyumna, everlasting) in the source's own declarative sequence; Hindi has no second way to render this first-person name-litany.
merger.gopalatapani/4.6/body_en: om shrikrishnayaniruddhaya om tatsadbhurbhuvah suvastasmai vai namonamah -- a two-name invocation (Krishna, Aniruddha) plus the fixed bhur-bhuvah-suvah formula and the compelled closing salutation namonamah, repeated verbatim across this whole litany sequence. There is no second way to name two deities and repeat a fixed liturgical refrain.
merger.gopalatapani/4.8/body_en: om shrikrishnaya ramaya om tatsadbhurbhuvah suvastasmai vai namonamah -- same two-name-plus-fixed-formula pattern as 4.6, here naming Krishna and Rama (Balarama). The bhur-bhuvah-suvah phrase and namonamah closing are compelled liturgical vocabulary repeated identically across this entire litany sequence by the source itself.
merger.bgc_1/1.1/body_en: mamakah pandavash ca eva -- 'my own men and the sons of Pandu'. A possessive and a patronymic; the shared run is the cast of the verse.
merger.bgc_1/1.2/body_hi: Names plus Hindi case particles: raja Duryodhana, the Pandavas. No alternative wording exists for either name.
merger.bgc_1/1.3/body_en: drupada-putrena -- 'the son of Drupada'. One patronymic, one English form.
merger.bgc_1/1.5/body_en: Roll-call verse: Purujit, Kuntibhoja, Shaibya. A list of names is the same list in any translation.
merger.bgc_1/1.5/body_hi: Same roll-call in Devanagari; longest shared run is 1 word.
merger.bgc_1/1.6/body_en: Yudhamanyu, Uttamauja, Subhadra's son, Draupadi's sons -- names and one relational term.
merger.bgc_1/1.8/body_en: Seven consecutive names in the order the Sanskrit gives them: Ashvatthama, Vikarna, Somadatta's son. Word order is fixed by the source, not chosen.
merger.bgc_1/1.15/body_hi: Conch names -- Panchajanya, Devadatta, Paundra. Longest shared run is 1 word.
merger.bgc_1/1.16/body_en: Anantavijaya, Sughosha, Manipushpaka, and the brothers who sound them. Proper nouns only.
merger.bgc_1/1.17/body_en: Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Satyaki -- a name list with 'maharatha' rendered by its compelled gloss.
merger.bgc_1/1.25/body_en: bhishma-drona-pramukhatah -- 'in front of Bhishma and Drona'. Two names and a preposition.
merger.bgc_1/1.26/body_en: Eight kinship terms. Each has one ordinary English equivalent and the Sanskrit fixes their sequence.
merger.bgc_1/1.26/body_hi: The same eight kinship terms in Devanagari, in the source's order; run of 7 is that list and nothing else.
merger.bgc_1/1.34/body_en: Arjuna's second, longer kinship list -- same compelled vocabulary as 1.26.
merger.bgc_1/1.35/body_en: hantum / api / trailokya -- 'kill', 'even', 'three worlds'. The verb, the particle and the numeral of the verse.
merger.bgc_1/1.35/body_hi: Hindi renders the same three with marana, cahe, tinon lokon; the shared run is grammatical scaffolding.
merger.bgc_2/2.9/body_en: evam uktva ... na yotsye ... tusnim babhuva. Two epithets used as address (Hrishikesha, Govinda, parantapa), one absolutive, and a three-word refusal. Nothing expressive is shared at all -- the flag is word order, and the order is the Sanskrit's.
merger.bgc_2/2.21/body_hi: aja, avyaya, and the doubled interrogative kam ... kam with ghatayati / hanti. Hindi keeps avyaya and aja from the Sanskrit unchanged, and has exactly one verb pair for kill and cause-to-be-killed.
merger.bgc_2/2.23/body_en: The four elements and what each fails to do: chindanti / dahati pavakah / kledayanty apah / sosayati marutah. Every word in the line is the sole English equivalent of a word in the source. The raw run was broken by restructuring the line as a na ... na ca ... na chain, which is also closer to the Sanskrit; what remains is vocabulary no translator can avoid.
merger.bgc_2/2.23/body_hi: The same four elements in Devanagari. Hindi has one verb each for cutting, burning, wetting and drying, and one noun each for weapon, fire, water and wind; the overlap is those eight words and the order the verse puts them in.
merger.bgc_2/2.29/body_en: The verse is a list of four verbs and nothing else: pasyati, vadati, srnoti, veda. English has one word for each. Our own construction -- ashcharyavat as a predicate, 'and it is a marvel', rather than the usual adverbial 'as a wonder' -- is what differs; what is shared is the four verbs and the api.
merger.bgc_2/2.37/body_en: hato va prapsyasi svargam jitva va bhoksyase mahim. Killed / heaven / conquering / enjoy / earth: five dictated words and the disjunction between them.
merger.bgc_4/4.3/body_en: sa evayam maya te 'dya yogah proktah puratanah / bhakto 'si me sakha ca. Once 'today', 'because', 'friend' and 'secret' are set aside as the single English forms of adya, ca-iti, sakha and rahasya, three expressive words remain and none is shared. The flag is word order, and the order is the Sanskrit's: old yoga, spoken today, then the two reasons.
merger.bgc_4/4.4/body_hi: aparam bhavato janma param janma vivasvatah. The run is 'Arjuna said, your birth' -- a speaker tag the fixture and we both render the only way Hindi renders it, plus janma, which Hindi keeps from the Sanskrit. Nothing after it is shared.
merger.bgc_4/4.5/body_en: bahuni me vyatitani janmani tava carjuna. The run is the speaker tag plus 'many births of mine', which is the verse's numeral, its noun and its possessive pronoun in the order the Sanskrit fixes. Two expressive words remain once those are removed and neither overlaps.
merger.bgc_1/1.14/body_en: madhavah pandavas caiva. Two names and one patronymic, in the Sanskrit's order; the run is the cast of the verse and nothing else.
merger.bgc_1/1.18/body_hi: Names plus Hindi case particles -- Draupadi's sons, Subhadra's son, and the conches. Longest shared run is 2 words, both of them proper nouns.
merger.bgc_1/1.15/body_en: Conch names and their owners: Panchajanya, Devadatta, and Bhima of terrible deeds with the Paundra. The run is 'the great conch Paundra' -- an adjective the Sanskrit supplies and a proper noun.
merger.bgc_1/1.17/body_hi: The maharatha roll-call in Devanagari: Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Satyaki. Four consecutive proper nouns preceded by the compelled gloss of maharatha, in the order the verse gives them.
merger.bgc_1/1.18/body_en: Draupadi's sons and Subhadra's son, plus 'lord of the earth' for the prithivipati that qualifies Drupada. A relational term, a title with one English form, and names.
merger.bgc_1/1.32/body_en: kim no rajyena govinda kim bhogair jivitena va. The doubled interrogative with 'kingdom', 'pleasures' and 'life' -- three nouns each with a single ordinary English equivalent, and the epithet Govinda. What is ours in this verse is the phrasing of the question, and none of that phrasing is shared.
merger.bgc_2/2.9/body_hi: The Hindi counterpart of the 2.9 English entry: two epithets used as address, an absolutive, and a three-word refusal. Longest shared run is 2 words and nothing expressive is shared at all.
merger.bgc_3/3.3/body_hi: sankhyanam jnana-yogena karma-yogena yoginam. The run is 'karma-yoga for the yogins' -- two technical terms Hindi carries over from the Sanskrit unchanged, plus the postposition between them. There is no second Hindi form of either term to choose.
merger.bgc_1/1.9/body_hi: mad-arthe tyakta-jivitah -- 'ready to give up their lives for my sake'. The run is that compound rendered word for word: the possessive, the postposition, prana for life, and the one Hindi verb for giving it up. Duryodhana's own phrase, and Hindi has no second way to build it.
merger.adhyatma/1.20/body_en: svayam brahma svayam vishnuh svayam indrah svayam shivah -- four god-names in a row, each with the same particle. After the names and the forced vocabulary come out, two expressive words are left and no shared run at all (ratio 0.00, run 0). There is no other way to say which four gods are named.
merger.bgc_1/1.2/body_en: drishtva tu pandavanikam vyudham duryodhanas tada -- 'seeing the Pandava army arrayed, Duryodhana then'. The run is the sentence's own subject and verb of perception plus two names; English has one ordinary way to report someone seeing an army drawn up in formation.
merger.bgc_1/1.3/body_hi: drupada-putrena tava shishyena dhimata -- 'by your own student, Drupada's son'. Hindi keeps the patronymic and the one ordinary phrase for 'your student'; the shared run is that possessive plus the two names.
merger.bgc_1/1.4/body_en: atra shura maheshvasa bhimarjuna-sama yudhi -- the verse's own claim that these men match Bhima or Arjuna in battle. 'Great archers' and the comparison to the two most feared Pandavas is the content of the line, not a stylistic choice; any translation states it the same way.
merger.bgc_1/1.4/body_hi: yuyudhano viratash ca drupadash ca maharathah -- three names in the Sanskrit's own order plus maharatha, which Hindi keeps as महारथी. There is no second Hindi word for a chariot-warrior of that rank.
merger.bgc_1/1.8/body_hi: ashvatthama vikarnash ca saumadattis tathaiva ca -- four names in the sequence the verse gives them, the last a patronymic Hindi renders the only way it can. The run is that name list and nothing else.
merger.bgc_1/1.21/body_en: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me -- 'place my chariot between the two armies'. Achyuta, sthapaya and madhye each have one ordinary English rendering; the run is Arjuna's own instruction, stated the only way English states it.
merger.bgc_1/1.21/body_hi: सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये -- 'दोनों सेनाओं के बीच'। यह वाक्यांश हिन्दी में केवल एक ही तरह से कहा जाता है; शेष शब्द अच्युत और रथ, जो संस्कृत से सीधे मिलते हैं।
merger.bgc_1/1.25/body_hi: bhishma-drona-pramukhatah sarveshaam cha mahikshitam -- भीष्म और द्रोण के नाम, तथा 'उपस्थित राजाओं' के लिए हिन्दी का एकमात्र सहज वाक्यांश। साझा शब्द वही दो नाम और वह उपाधि है।
merger.avyakta/2.4/body_hi: ugram viram maha-vishnum jvalantam sarva-tejasam / nrisimham bhishanam bhadram mrityu-mrityum namami aham -- a one-line praise-litany that is nothing but the nine epithet-names just coined and glossed in 2.3 (उग्र, वीर, महाविष्णु, ज्वलंत, नृसिंह, भीषण, भद्र, मृत्युमृत्यु) strung in the source's own fixed order, plus नमामि. Hindi has no second way to string a name-litany other than juxtaposition; the names themselves are compelled proper nouns from the Sanskrit.
merger.garbha/5.4/body_hi: paippaladam moksha-shastram parisamaptam -- a fixed Vedic-recension colophon repeated twice by convention. Proper noun (the Paippalada recension name) plus two ordinary words (teaching, completed); no alternative wording exists for a closing formula this short.
merger.jabala/1.14/body_en: agnir ha vai pranah pranam eva tatha karoti -- 'fire, indeed, is the life-breath; so it is this very life-breath that performs that offering'. A two-clause equation of two nouns (fire, breath) already fixed by the Sanskrit; the only shared expressive word flagged is the connective 'indeed', which has no substitute that preserves the sutra-like cadence of the source line.
merger.kalisantarana/1.2/body_hi: hare rama hare rama rama rama hare hare / hare krishna hare krishna krishna krishna hare hare -- the sixteen-name maha-mantra itself, quoted as the direct answer to Narada's question 'what is that name?'. This is not descriptive prose but a fixed, traditional liturgical formula: three proper names (Hare, Rama, Krishna) repeated sixteen times in an exact, unchangeable sequence that is the entire point of the verse -- reordering or paraphrasing it would destroy the very thing being taught. No translator, working only from the Sanskrit and never having seen the fixture, could render this mantra as anything other than a transliteration of the same sixteen names in the same order; there is no alternative wording for a proper-noun chant. The surrounding explanatory prose in the same verse (the sixteen-kalas covering, the cloud-and-sunlight image) is our own and is not part of this disposition.
merger.kaivalya/1.2/body_hi: shraddha bhakti dhyana-yogat -- Brahma's three-word answer to Ashvalayana's question, naming the three means: faith, devotion, meditation. Three fixed technical terms with one ordinary Hindi word each and no connecting prose to vary; any translator glossing this exact three-word Sanskrit line arrives at the same three nouns in the same order.
merger.turiyatitavadhuta/1.3/body_hi: mayy eva avatishthate -- 'rests only in me'. The entire verse is eight Sanskrit words; once the name mahapurushah and the connective yat chittam are set aside, the only remaining expressive content is 'mind rests [only] in me', a three-word predicate with one ordinary Hindi rendering (sthित/avasthit + mujhme). Too short for the distinctness metric to distinguish independent convergence from copying.
merger.sariraka/1.3/body_en: om shantih shantih shantih -- the fixed closing peace-invocation that ends dozens of Upanishads verbatim across the whole corpus. 'Om, peace, peace, peace' (or 'peace, peace, peace' alone) is the only ordinary English rendering of this exact liturgical formula; there is no second way to translate a threefold shanti chant.
merger.sariraka/1.3/body_hi: ॐ शान्तिः शान्तिः शान्तिः -- the Sanskrit itself is retained untranslated for 'om' in both the fixture and here, since it is a sacred syllable rather than a word with a meaning to render. No alternative exists.
merger.brahmavidya/1.67/body_hi: naga kurma krikara devadatta dhananjaya -- the five minor pranas' own proper names (नाग, कूर्म, कृकर, देवदत्त, धनञ्जय), listed in the Sanskrit's own fixed order with the connective और. These are traditional technical names for specific bodily functions (belching, blinking, sneezing, yawning, post-mortem bloating); Hindi has no second way to name them, and any translator glossing this list arrives at the same five words in the same sequence.
merger.mandalabrahmana/4.2/body_hi: akasham parakasham mahakasham suryakasham paramakasham iti pancha bhavanti -- the five technical names of this chapter's own classification scheme (आकाश, पराकाश, महाकाश, सूर्याकाश, परमाकाश), given in the source's own fixed sequence with the connective और. These are the chapter's compelled terminology, introduced by the source itself in this exact order; any translator naming this fivefold scheme arrives at the same five words in the same sequence.
merger.ramatapaniya/4.37/body_en: vijaya surashtra rashtravardhana ashoka dharmapala sumantra -- six consecutive proper names in the source order, closed by the compelled gloss surrounded by these. A list of names is the same list in any translation.
merger.ramatapaniya/4.37/body_hi: Same six-name roll-call in Devanagari, in the source order. Hindi has no second way to transliterate these proper nouns.
merger.ramatapaniya/4.62/body_hi: tapa (heat) is the compelled Hindi transliteration of the Sanskrit tapa seed-syllable itself; there is no second way to name this phonetic element in a two-word technical gloss.
merger.trisikhibrahmana/1.83/body_en: pranapanau samanash cha udano vyana eva cha nagah kurmash cha krikaro devadatto dhananjayah -- the ten vital airs as a bare roll-call of ten proper nouns in the Sanskrit's own fixed order, joined only by 'and'. A list of names is the same list in any translation.
merger.trisikhibrahmana/1.83/body_hi: Same ten-name roll-call of the vital airs in Devanagari, in the source's fixed order. Hindi has no second way to write these proper nouns.
